extracted.intended_audience: scholars, students and activists in sociology/political theory studying race, urban poverty, policing and post‑colonial/imperialist relations
extracted.subtask_description: Critical sociological analysis of black urban crime ('mugging') and its political significance, situating it within capitalist accumulation, colonial history, class formation, and movements (e.g., Fanonism, Black Power, Panthers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial reserve army (Marxian rhythm)
rubrics_metrics.description: The industrial reserve army of the unemployed is as fundamental to the laws of capitalist accumulation as the size of the productive 'labour-army'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Marx's argument about rhythms of accumulation to both metropolis and colonial hinterlands; consider differences in size/significance of unemployed, wageless, semi-employed and marginalised sectors, but retain the reserve-army logic when analysing formation of surplus labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitute reserve armies: women and migrant labour
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern capitalism has made use of two principal 'reserve' sources: women and migrant labour. 'The solution to these problems adopted by West European capitalism has been the employment of immigrant workers from under-developed areas ...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace phases: productive expansion (labour sucked into production), restrictive practices (forcing parts of reserve to remain in homelands), and phases of control and expulsion in crisis; treat migrant workers as a permanent basis of the modern industrial reserve army where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double positioning of the black working class
rubrics_metrics.description: The black working class as a whole belongs to two, different, though intersecting, histories: the history of Caribbean labour and the history of the British working class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing potential politics and trajectories of black class strata, hold both histories in mind — colonial experience shapes survival strategies, outlooks and modes of class struggle that may resemble lumpen forms but are better understood via prior colonial history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heterogeneity and modes of the 'rootless poor' / outcasts
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical urban poor/outcast are unemployed, of low status, living a marginal economic existence, usually in a distinct area, and generally regarded as 'social outcasts'. Distinguish those born into outcast status from those who have become outcasts, and those permanently/semi-permanently unemployed from those who never were employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse internal distinctions (born vs becoming outcast, migrant trajectories, petty-trading, crime, 'penny capitalism') rather than treating the group as homogeneous 'lumpenproletariat'.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Surplus population' types (Obregon)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obregon identifies 'floating' sectors (drawn into and expelled from employment), 'latent' sectors (rural workers drifting into cities), 'intermittent' sectors (permanent but irregular employment), 'lumpenproletariat' (vagrants, prostitutes, criminals) and the 'paupers' (totally unemployed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these internal categories to specify which form of surplus population is present; note Obregon's argument that in some contexts the surplus population ceases to be a 'reserve army' because re-employment is unlikely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fanon's thesis on lumpenproletariat and violence
rubrics_metrics.description: Fanon argued that violence binds the colonised together and frees the native from inferiority; he saw the peasantry and the lumpenproletariat as key revolutionary forces: 'the lumpenproletariat ... constitutes one of the most spontaneous and the most revolutionary forces of a colonised people.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider Fanon's view that expressive/collective violence has social-organisational functions and psychological effects, but also note he advocated organised violence (not merely unorganised crime) and that lumpen must be 'urged on from behind' by organisation and leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of revolutionary nationalists / 'illegalists' as vanguard
rubrics_metrics.description: Revolutionary nationalists — the 'illegalists' — retreat to the countryside, identify with the peasantry and come to provide the vanguard stratum in the revolutionary coalition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating revolutionary strategy in colonial/underdeveloped settings, include the interaction between peasant-based guerrilla strategy and urban lumpen forces; assess capacity for political training and integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposition of Fanonism to Black movements (internal colony framing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The identification with Africa led Black American movements to rediscover historical/cultural identity and to reconceptualise the ghetto as an 'internal colony' — the 'Third World' within the 'First World'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 'internal colony' lens to analyse shifts from reformist/integrationist politics to revolutionary/separatist politics and to understand cultural-nationalist and radical strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panthers' dual strategy: politicisation of unemployed and community self-help
rubrics_metrics.description: The Panthers recruited the unemployed and sought to provide a political alternative to hustling via a 'lumpen politics' combining armed self-defence and community self-help (establishing alternative social structures, rudiments of an alternative social life).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate both aspects: armed self-defence as immediate protective practice responding to police repression, and community programmes aimed at creating organisation, discipline and alternative livelihoods; recognise the need for political practice to root in and transform daily conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Secondariness' — race-class positionality
rubrics_metrics.description: The position which results from the combination of race and class is called a position of secondariness: black labour is roughly coterminous with the white working class yet segmentally differentiated and subordinated through race across institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse how racism operates not only as discriminatory attitudes but as specific mechanisms reproducing black labour across education, housing, occupations — race both structures oppression and channels forms of resistance/consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crime as structural consequence versus political expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Crime often arises as a 'symbiotic adaptation to deprivation' and is not inherently a political act; yet in certain circumstances acts like snatching or robbery against white victims can give 'a muffled and displaced expression' to the experience of permanent exclusion and oppositional class consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reduce political content to criminal forms; distinguish adaptive/survival crime from acts that function as expressions of oppositional consciousness, and always 'go behind' the criminal acts to the producing conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wagelessness as central analytical condition
rubrics_metrics.description: The connection lies not in 'crime' per se but in the position of wagelessness of the black proletariat; wagelessness may indicate a quasi-political consciousness such as 'refusal to work' and may make crime one applicable mode of survival.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting criminalised behaviour, interrogate wagelessness: its political interpretations (refusal as nascent mass-worker consciousness) and its practical consequences (survival strategies, potential recruitment ground for political projects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid permanent ascription of political form to a social sector (context specificity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms of consciousness, modes of struggle and positions in the revolutionary spectrum cannot be permanently ascribed to any one sector; 'Lima is not Bissau, and Bissau is not Calcutta.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make context-specific assessments (historical, cultural, social) rather than generalising Fanonist or other theses; compare Cabral's more sober, locality-sensitive assessments with universalising claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyse whole class to understand criminalised fraction
rubrics_metrics.description: The criminal acts labelled 'muggings' and patterns of black crime should drive analysis back to consideration of the whole black class — the black sub-proletariat — of which criminals are a criminalised fraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and strategy must address the class as a whole to prevent sizeable sections becoming permanently criminalised; link micro-level criminal behaviour to macro-level structures reproducing sub-proletarian positions.
